newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia to pay out $1 billion to farmers.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia to pay out $1 billion to farmers.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's intention to pay four billion riyals ($1.07 billion) owed to 50,000 cash-strapped farmers will not lure them back to the formerly lucrative and subsidised sector, analysts said on Thursday.

"The payment will help setting farmers' personal finances right. It will serve to accelerate the trend of moving away from subsidised crops -- grains -- to water-efficient production of other crops," said a farm analyst by telephone from Riyadh.
The state's Grain Silos and Flour Mills Organisation (GSFMO) said it would start repaying four billion riyals on Saturday.
"The cheques have been prepared and distributed to points of payment," said director general Saleh al-Suliman this week.

Amid huge Gulf War liabilities and soft oil prices until early 1996, the desert kingdom fell behind on payments to farmers, causing painful cash crunches. The first sign of relief came in August when it repaid three billion riyals in arrears to holders of special farmers certificates issued early this year.
But agriculture analysts say the damage from the long-delayed payments is done and little can now prompt more grain sowing in the world's biggest barley-importing nation.
Years of mounting debt coupled with sharp cuts in subsidies have changed the face of the sector, sending those who invested in agriculture mainly to reap generous state subsidies fleeing.

"People were badly burnt. A lot of the pivots have broken down in the past few years. It would not be easy to get them back up. A price of 1,500 riyals (a tonne of wheat) from 4,000 a few years ago is not a tremendous incentive to plant either," a farmer said.
Analysts estimate the 1996 harvest yielded 1.0 to 1.2 million tonnes of wheat against a quota of 1.3 million. Local consumption is about 1.8 million tonnes. The gap is met with declining stocks.
John Wilson, director of the U.S. Agricultural Trade Office in Riyadh, estimates the 1996 barley harvest at about 450,000 tonnes, compared with a quota of one million tonnes.
"The 550,000 tonne shortfall is because there haven't been prompt payments and also the fact that quotas are allocated mainly to small farmers who have higher costs of production," he said.
"The costs of production of small farmers are often as high as the support price given for barley," he added.
The barley support price is $267 but after deductions for a religious tax and foreign matter the actual price is $240.

Although 1997 quotas are not yet out, analysts said they may be higher than 1996 as record wheat prices earlier this year jolted the state into rethinking its plans to gradually cut output in a bid to reduce vast consumption of scarce water.
"High cereal prices gave the government a fright. The rate at which the government is buying from farmers was at one stage only slightly higher than the world price," said a farm consultant.
Global wheat prices have fallen from early-1996 peaks, but wheat is still trading at double what it was three years ago.

"Maybe higher prices will prompt on-time payment. They want to cut down on the possibility of having to import wheat. They don't want to be caught in a position where they have to import. They'll have to pay on time to get the farmers to grow it," said a farmer.

"I've got a feeling the 1997 quota will be raised. They might even put restrictions on alfalfa because water use is up even though grain production is down. Exporting alfalfa is like exporting water," said an analyst of the trend towards growing more alfalfa for export to dairies in neighbouring countries. ($1=3.75 riyals)
